name: BMS-564929

lead: BMS-564929 is a highly potent oral SARM that muscle-building users mention for strong muscle stimulation with little prostate stimulation. Bristol-Myers Squibb developed it for age-related decline.

It binds the androgen receptor with subnanomolar affinity and is selective over other steroid receptors. A 2007 study in castrated rats reported strong skeletal muscle stimulation with comparatively little prostate effect. It entered Phase I, which was discontinued, and no results are public.

paras: Users who mention it describe taking it orally as a research chemical alongside resistance training for lean-mass phases. There is no published human protocol.
Strong suppression of luteinizing hormone has been reported, so natural testosterone signalling can drop. Human safety is unpublished. It is unapproved and banned in sport.

angle.text: BMS-564929 is a highly potent SARM that muscle-building users mention for strong muscle stimulation with little prostate effect. It binds the androgen receptor very tightly, which drove muscle growth in castrated rats. It was developed for age-related decline, and its Phase I trial was discontinued.

lead: BMS-564929 (also PS-178990) is a potent, orally active, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator developed by Bristol-Myers Squibb for age-related functional decline in men [1][2]. A 2007 Endocrinology study reported a subnanomolar androgen receptor affinity, selectivity over other steroid receptors, and strong stimulation of skeletal muscle with comparatively little prostate stimulation in castrated rats [1].
It advanced to early clinical trials, but Wikipedia reports that the Phase I trial was discontinued, and no results were identified [2][3]. It is unapproved and SARMs are prohibited in sport [3].

paras: The compound is a highly potent androgen receptor agonist with no significant interaction with SHBG or aromatase, and in castrated rats it showed dose-dependent muscle effects with hypostimulation of the prostate [1]. Wikipedia reports about 20-fold functional muscle-over-prostate selectivity and notes that it suppresses luteinizing hormone far more than testosterone does [2].

No studies found reporting human results. The compound entered early trials, which were reported discontinued [2][3]. Published research otherwise consists of the rat study and analytical papers on urine detection and mass spectrometry [1][4].

No human safety data were published. Reviews of the class describe elevated liver enzymes, reduced HDL cholesterol and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in some trials, case reports linking recreational SARM use to liver injury, and unknown cardiovascular risk; the US FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs. [3]
